en: Commentary on the Treatises of Sengzhao, Scroll One. Preface.
Composed by Shi Yuankang.
The author of this preface to the *Treatises of Sengzhao* is Dharma Master Da of Xiaozhaoti Monastery. Regarding this single treatise, the text...
It consists of two sections:
the first is the introductory text,
and the second is the main body of the treatise.
Regarding what is now called the "Preface to the Treatises of Sengzhao":
it was composed by the Dharma Master Śramaṇa Sengzhao of Chang’an during the reign of Yao Xing of the Later Qin dynasty.
He composed treatises such as "The Fundamental Principle of Non-transmigration";
these were named after their author,
and are thus called the "Treatises of Sengzhao."
This preface describes the intent of the treatises composed by Master Sengzhao;
therefore, it is called a "Preface" (xu).
The *Erya* states:
The east and west walls are called the *xu* (partitions).
Guo Xiang’s commentary states:
"They are used to order and distinguish between the interior and the exterior."
Now, Master Da has set forth the intent of the treatise as its gradual unfolding,
just as the eastern and western walls constitute the sequence for a dwelling.
Therefore, it is called the "Preface.
As for the statement that it was composed by Dharma Master Da of Xiao Zhaoti,
he was from Jiangning County in Runzhou.
It was originally the commandery of Danyang,
beginning from the Wu dynasty and continuing through the six successive dynasties of Song, Qi, Liang, and Chen.
Buddhism flourished there;
monasteries and viharas stood side by side with their rafters and eaves joined together,
their names intermingled.
Such instances occur frequently.
For example, at Zhuangyan Monastery,
there were both the Great Zhuangyan and the Wondrous Zhuangyan.
Regarding Zhaoti Temple, there are both a Great Zhaoti and a Small Zhaoti.
The Great Zhaoti was constructed during the Liang dynasty;
the Small Zhaoti was constructed during the Jin dynasty.
Dharma Master Huida was a person of the Chen dynasty.
He was a monk of Xiaozhaoti Monastery.
Among those renowned as "Da" during the Chen period, he was the most distinguished.
It was not merely one person;
therefore, he designated the monastery by name to distinguish it.
Some original texts simply state that it was compiled by Xiaozhaoti;
"compiled" (zhuàn) means to collect and assemble,
not to compose from scratch.
One should say "composed" (作);
one should not say "compiled" (撰).
When it is simply stated as "the Small Caitya" without mentioning its name, [it refers to this].
In the region east of the Yangtze River, they revered Dharma Master Jing;
thus, they did not call him by his personal name,
but referred to him solely by the name of his monastery.
However, this Dharma Master was not yet proficient in literary style; thus,
the prefaces he composed for his treatises...
There are many mediocre compositions that merely recount the tenets of the treatises;
yet they are not without their own systematic order.
I value your elegant intention;
it shall be explained as follows.
I hope that you, a person of broad learning, will not find cause for reproach.
Huida leads the ignorant and lowly; within this preface, it is divided into two sections.
The first briefly clarifies the original cause for its composition.
Next, the preface formally sets forth the fundamental tenets of the *Zhao lun*.
This is divided into six sections based on the preceding text.
The first section presents the title of the treatise.
The second is praising the beauty of the person;
the third is rejoicing at having encountered them;
the fourth is refuting and censuring their faults.
The fifth section sets forth the original circumstances;
the sixth clarifies the intent of the preface.
Now, as for the word "following" (shuài):

"Huida" is his name.
As for Chang'an:
the Qin dynasty's original capital was Xianyang;
the Han dynasty moved the capital to Chang'an.
Cháng'ān was the name of a district during the Qin dynasty;
it was named after its original designation and was called Cháng'ān County.
Regarding the Dharma Master Śramaṇa Sengzhao:
the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gaoseng zhuan) compiled by Dharma Master Jiao of Jiexiang Temple in Kuaiji during the Liang dynasty states that Śramaṇa Sengzhao was a native of Jingzhao.
His family was poor, so he made his living by hiring himself out as a copyist.
Consequently, while engaged in transcribing texts,
he extensively surveyed the classics and histories.
He had thoroughly mastered the classics and histories and took profound delight in the profound and subtle mysteries;
he always regarded the teachings of Laozi and Zhuangzi as the essentials of his heart.
Once, while reading the "Dao De" chapters of Laozi, I sighed and said:
"It is indeed beautiful;
yet, it lacks the method for attaining spiritual transcendence and dissolving worldly burdens."
It was still not yet complete.
Later, upon seeing the ancient *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*,
he received it with joy, wearing it upon his head, and upheld it.
He studied and contemplated it with great devotion,
saying, "Only now do I know where to turn for refuge. Consequently,
he left the household life to study the Way.
He was well-versed in the Vaipulya sutras and also proficient in the Tripitaka;
even during his youth, his reputation resounded throughout Guanzhong.
At that time, among those who vied for advancement,
there were none who did not suspect him of having attained his early success through improper means; consequently,
they all traveled from a thousand li away, carrying their own provisions.
Upon entering the pass, he engaged in a spirited debate;
Sengzhao was both possessed of profound and subtle talent and skilled in eloquent discourse.
He seized the opportunity to blunt their sharpness,
never lingering or hesitating;
at that time, he was a veteran scholar in the capital.
As for the eminent scholars beyond the passes,
there were none who did not come forth with their sharp wit and defiant spirit, only to be defeated and humbled.
Later, Kumārajīva arrived at Guzang.
From the time Huìzhào first followed him,
Kumārajīva praised and admired him boundlessly.
When Kumārajīva traveled to Cháng'ān, [Huìzhào followed him there as well].
Sengzhao also returned with them.
Yao Xing then invited Sengzhao, Sengrui,
and others into the Xiaoyao Garden.
In carefully determining the scriptures and treatises,
Sengzhao [observed] that since the Sage had long since passed away,
the textual meanings had become confused and disordered.
The interpretations of former scholars were occasionally erroneous;
upon consulting with Kumārajīva,
I realized even more.
Based on the fundamental principles of our school,
I have composed the "Treatise on the Non-Transmigration of Things" and the "Treatise on the Non-Emptiness of Reality."
When the *Prajñānāmamūlamadhyamakakārikā* was finally presented to Kumārajīva,
he read it and praised it as excellent.
He then said to Sengzhao,
"I do not need to thank you for your understanding;
as for your departure, I shall embrace you."
At that time, Liu Yimin of Mount Lu saw this treatise by Sengzhao and sighed in admiration, saying:
"I did not expect that among those in monastic robes there would yet be another like Zhongping."
He presented it to Master Huiyuan,
who then leaned on his desk and sighed, saying,
"I have never encountered the like before."
Because they had together searched through, savored,
and further exchanged [their views on it],
after Kumārajīva passed away, [the text remained].
In mourning for his eternal departure,
he redoubled his efforts in contemplation and subsequently composed the "Treatise on the Namelessness of Nirvana."
Thus did Yao Xing, the ruler of Qin,
respond with earnest sincerity,
offering extensive praise and exposition.
He immediately issued an edict to have it transcribed and distributed it among his sons and nephews;
such was the esteem in which it was held by the people of that time.
In the tenth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty,
he passed away in Chang’an at the age of thirty-one.

Dharma Master Rui, in his Preface to the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, stated:
"Now, the myriad existents are rooted in the process of being born."
That which gives rise to arising is itself without arising;
transformation begins at the inception of things,
yet that which initiates this inception is itself without beginning.
Thus, that which is without birth and without beginning is the nature of things;
birth and beginning do not stir within this nature.
While the myriad phenomena are arrayed externally,

The Perfectly Awakened One perceived that false thoughts arise from within;

He understood that the stagnation in existence results from delusion.
Therefore, Prajñā serves as its mirror.

The principle transcends the surface of words,

The treatise contains six schools,

The first school is the School of Non-Being;

Regarding the statement that there are twelve,

Shi Sengjing of Xiadinglin Monastery composed the *Six Schools’ Treatise on True Reality* (*Shixiang liujia lun*).
First, he established a hypothetical interlocutor’s question regarding the single essence of the two truths,

The first [type of emptiness] is that which is empty because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) do not exist in reality;
ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) claim that conditioned phenomena exist,
whereas emptiness is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
The first [position] holds that existence is conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The second school takes the emptiness of the nature of form (*rūpa*) as emptiness,
while regarding the substance of form as existent.
The third school regards the absence of mind when conditions are absent as emptiness,
and the presence of mind when conditions are present as existence.
The fourth school regards the arising of the mind from conditions as emptiness.

The fifth school maintains that there is a distinct essence of mind existing apart from conditions as "existence," and that the emptiness postulated by those with false views is "emptiness," while the mind produced by causes and conditions is "existence."
The sixth school holds that the substance which is the basis of form is empty in reality,
yet is conventionally designated as "existent" within worldly discourse. Thus,
there have been six schools previously.
Later there were six schools, which together constitute twelve schools.
Therefore it is said: "Yuan Yan [established] the twelve [schools]."
